quote: Could I regenerate this knowledge if it were somehow deleted from my mind?
content: The test targets understanding, not where a thought came from. "If the thought originally came from outside, make sure it comes from inside as well" allows every thought to start as testimony. It asks that you learn the thought well enough to rebuild and extend it, as the shepherd's apprentice must understand the pebbles to know what to do with an extra one. Einstein learned Riemannian geometry from Grossmann and then used it to write field equations Grossmann could not, which is the test passed. Brute facts such as the date of Hastings are not what the essay has in mind; its examples are theorems, mechanisms and the meaning of "wave." The learning literature supports it: generating and explaining material to oneself, rather than just receiving it, produces better retention and transfer (Slamecka & Graf 1978; Chi et al. 1989).

quote: then you do not have any beliefs about beavers, true or false
content: The point is Davidson's own, from "Thought and Talk": "how clear are we that the ancients—some ancients—believed that the earth was flat? This earth? Well, this earth of ours is part of the solar system..." With enough false belief, a belief loses its object (1975, book chapter, no DOI). The causal theory of reference does not escape the problem. Evans's "Madagascar" case, a name that moved from part of the African mainland to the island through a traveller's error, shows that reference follows the dominant body of information once the misinformation is great enough (Evans 1973, Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, supp. vol., no DOI). The child told about white desert giants may refer to beavers, but she cannot recognize one, and that is the essay's concern. The Wittgenstein image of the idle wheel says the same thing.

quote: If all proofs of the Pythagorean Theorem were deleted from my mind, could I re-prove it? I think so.
content: The essay flags the limit of its own self-report: "That's harder to boast, without putting it to the test." The test is meant to be run, and for the Pythagorean theorem it can be, with a pencil in ten minutes. Attempting to regenerate knowledge is also the best-supported study technique in cognitive psychology: retrieval practice beats rereading by large margins on delayed tests (Roediger & Karpicke 2006). It also defeats the illusion of explanatory depth, because it forces the explanation to be produced (Rozenblit & Keil 2002). The regeneration test is the remedy for the very illusion the note cites against it.
